take: The White House ruling out a diesel export ban whilst prices surge above $6.50 is the key crude/products story, as it removes the tail risk of a policy intervention that would have upended global distillate flows and instead leaves the market to clear through price alone, with elevated crack spreads already flagged by the EIA as a driver of pump prices. The second theme is the Strait of Hormuz crisis, now seven months old, where ship-to-ship transfers and bypass pipelines have become the primary export route at steep cost, a seafarer was killed aboard the Cape Dao capesize and a cargo vessel was struck and set ablaze, turning roughly 20% of global LNG supply into interruptible volumes and adding a permanent freight and insurance premium to every Gulf barrel. On positioning, Onex DMCC has snapped up at least five VLCCs and Canada’s oil patch is on track for its biggest M&A wave in a decade, whilst the EIA forecasts record US crude output of 13.8m b/d in 2026 and US LNG exports already averaged 17.4 Bcf/d in H1, so the supply side is loosening even as the freight and risk premium tightens. The cross-market link to watch is bunker versus gasoil, with the Ship & Bunker viewpoint warning on uncapped late-payment interest and short quality-claim deadlines precisely when fuel prices have doubled, meaning higher distillate cracks transmit straight into voyage economics and tonne-mile demand. In the next 24 hours, watch whether Hormuz transits deteriorate further after today’s casualties and whether the diesel export ban chatter is truly dead, because any revival would blow out the US Gulf Coast distillate basis and reshape Atlantic basin arb flows overnight.

items.title: Public companies produce most U.S. crude oil and natural gas
items.summary: Publicly traded companies represent a tiny share of the total number of companies producing crude oil and natural gas in the United States, but they make up a large share of U.S. production. In 2025, publicly traded companies accounted for just 2% of about 12,000 oil and natural gas producers but produced 68% of the crude oil and natural gas in the Lower 48 states.

items.title: What goes into diesel prices?
items.summary: The price of distillate fuel oil, often sold as diesel, is driven by the price of crude oil, retail margins, distribution costs, taxes, and crack spreads, the indicator we use for refining margins. Tight global supplies of distillate fuel oil and elevated crude oil prices have driven prices higher in recent months.
